overview: This file assembles State Department filing sheets and two substantive consular reports on wages, hours, employment, and labor conditions in Japanese-ruled Taiwan. Hayward G. Hill’s confidential 1931 report presents official wage data for manufacturing, mining, forestry, and agriculture, discusses unemployment and the anticipated labor-market effects of restarting the Sun Moon Lake hydroelectric project, and explains the limitations of its government-derived sources. John H. Ketcham’s 1934 report updates wage scales across numerous trades and describes ethnic and gender pay disparities, working hours, unionization, labor regulation, compensation, housing, insurance, and pensions. A final 1938 cross-reference points to a later report that is not present in this bundle.

subfiles.title: Hill report on wages and unemployment in Taiwan
subfiles.to: U.S. Department of State; copy to the U.S. Consulate General, Tokyo
subfiles.about: A statistical and analytical report on wages, hours, unemployment, and labor supply in Taiwan in 1929–1931.
subfiles.summary: Hill compiles official wage figures for manufacturing, mining, forestry, and agriculture, generally covering 1929 and the first half of 1930, with comparisons among Japanese and Formosan male and female workers. The tables show workdays commonly ranging from eight to eleven hours and indicate that subsequent wage revisions had generally been slight and downward. The report predicts that renewed work on the Sun Moon Lake hydroelectric project could eliminate unemployment and strengthen workers’ demands for higher pay, while noting that only locally unavailable skilled labor would be imported from Japan. Its confidential source discussion explains the dependence on Taiwan Government General officials and the limited availability of labor statistics.

subfiles.title: Ketcham report on current wages and labor conditions in Taiwan
subfiles.to: Commercial Office, U.S. Department of State
subfiles.about: An updated survey of wages by trade and of employment practices, labor protections, and welfare provisions in Taiwan.
subfiles.summary: Ketcham presents official wage scales updated through the first half of 1933 for a wide range of industrial, artisanal, construction, transport, domestic-service, and food-processing occupations. He emphasizes that Japanese workers were more often foremen or skilled laborers, that Formosan Chinese supplied most labor, and that women commonly earned about half the male rate. The report describes approximately ten-hour workdays, minimal rest, the absence of labor and workers’ compensation laws comparable to Japan’s, official discouragement of unions, and limited overtime, housing, insurance, pension, and customary injury-compensation arrangements. Copies were distributed to the Department of Labor, the commercial attaché, and the consulate general.

interest: Shows 1930s colonial Taiwan's wage structure by ethnicity and industry, and state labor-welfare and union policy.
